article.title: Faced With Record Fires, France Skimps on Fire Crews
article.author: Marlon Ettinger
article.content: For thirty years, Patrice Hureaux has fought fires in his forest-covered corner of southwestern France. Every summer, he and his team work diligently to put out fires in the woods right as they start. Landes, where he lives and works, is one of the most wooded of France’s 101 local départements , with fully two-thirds of its territory covered in trees. He and his colleagues have their work cut out for them, but the vigilance is worth it. “It’s much easier to put out a fire when it starts than to let it build in intensity,” Hureaux told me earlier this month. “After, you need much more water and much more resources.” This summer has presented a particularly grueling challenge for France’s volunteer firefighters like Hureaux, as well as its understaffed professional forces. Out-of-control fires have swept across stretches of land four times as large as Paris, causing a quarter of a million people to flee their homes, injuring hundreds of firefighters, and leaving four firefighters dead. For months this summer, France groaned under a series of hellish heat waves that at times made parts of the country the hottest places in the world. Temperatures have soared dizzyingly above 105 degrees Fahrenheit, with catastrophic effects for the country’s wildlife — think lakes filled with dead fish and mysterious bird deaths. Nearly everywhere starting in late June, vegetation turned eerily autumnal, with wilting trees shedding amarillo and amber leaves to skitter across sunbaked streets, and springy green grass shriveling into dry, faded-yellow straw. In Landes, Hureaux explained, a rainy autumn, winter, and spring meant that lots of vegetation grew. Ferns and other undergrowth covered the forest floor, then a storm at the end of the winter downed tree branches and soaked the soil. The loose, waterlogged ground made it easy for wind to pull pine trees up and across pathways the firefighters need to access the forest and put out flames before they burn out of control. But from the start of summer, as heat waves rolled in one after another, all this abundant material dried up. By mid-August, it was the perfect fuel for a conflagration that burned nearly two thousand hectares and caused six hundred locals to be evacuated from their homes. As the endless heat waves broke last week, the fires have begun to come under control, and residents have been returned to their homes. But Hureaux is convinced that the new climatic conditions mean that every year could see fires just as frequent and intense. “The forest has changed. There’s no reason to believe it will stop. . . . I think there’ll be more episodes like this. . . . all this has changed our working conditions a little,” Hureaux told me. Quarter-Century Shift According to an analysis by Reporterre , there were thirty times more fires in France by July this year than there had been in all of 2010. Ten times as much land has burned too — at least 119,000 hectares. One hectare is equal to ten thousand square meters — about the size of a Manhattan city block. Reporterre’s analysis, based on a dataset that tracks significant fires of over thirty hectares, shows the dramatic explosion in fires over the past twenty-five years. In 2010 there were nine such fires. As of mid-July this year, there have been 308, outpacing the previous peak of 304 fires, from 2019. Before that past peak, there had never been over a hundred. In the past, the threat of fires has been largely confined to France’s hotter Mediterranean coast and hinterlands. But the national weather service has warned that the projected 4°C rise by the end of the century could create a generalized fire risk across the country, including in the densely populated Paris metropolitan region or the wet banks of the Loire valley. In July, firefighters fought an out-of-control wildfire forty miles south of Paris in the Fontainebleau forest which burned about 10 percent of its surface area. At the same time as these deadly weather conditions are becoming an established feature of the climate, across the national territory, firefighters say that there’s another factor making the situation even worse. They point to a serious shortage in manpower and resources needed to confront the new reality. Megafeux “I don’t like the term ‘mega-fires,’” Rémy Chabbouh told me, referring to a common description of the fires by the French media this summer. A spokesman for the SUD union of professional firefighters, Chabbouh says that the term wrongly implies that there’s nothing that can be done about the fires, casting them as a “diabolic” force of nature. That isn’t the case, Chabbouh, a longtime firefighter himself, insisted. In 2022, a similar wave of massive out-of-control fires swept across France from the Gironde in the South to Brittany in the North. Even the Brocéliande — a misty, moist, moss-covered forest that is the setting of many of the Arthurian legends — went up in flames (this year, access is currently limited because of extreme dryness and the threat of fire). For the first time, all of France was burning at once. Firefighters rung the alarm bell and, after a series of working groups and consultative meetings, put a raft of propositions on the interior minister’s desk in September 2025. In France, the SDIS national firefighting service is under this ministry’s authority. Now, with a budget fight coming early next month, Chabbouh says the proposals have gone ignored. He and other professional firefighter union leaders met with the current Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez on August 13 for discussions on the budget but faced a frustrating two-hour conversation where Nuñez effectively told them nothing about what measures the funding bill would contain. “There’s been nothing, nothing at all,” Chabbouh told me, joking that Nuñez has been using the report to prop up a table for the past year. Nuñez justified his decision by saying that lawmakers in the National Assembly need to take a look at it before he shares it with union leaders and the public on September 8. Chabbouh said there’s no reason for the firefighter unions to hold off on striking given that there are zero guarantees that the budget will contain the resources they need. A union response is already scheduled, with a three-day occupation of Paris’s Place de la République to protest against government inaction planned to begin on September 26. More People One of the chief concerns firefighters have is a lack of manpower, especially when so many firefighters are facing exhaustion and injuries like smoke intoxication from prolonged exposure across days-long battles against the flames. By early August, most firefighters in Bouches-du-Rhône were already much more tired that they usually are, Laurent Guilloteau told me. Guilloteau, who is a subofficer in the SDIS and had a long career fighting fires on the front lines in the South of France, told me that the frequency and unprecedented geographic spread of the fires has contributed to that exhaustion. In his firehouse, ten people had already suffered from smoke intoxication. This year, Guilloteau told me, firefighters from Bouches-du-Rhône have already fought fires in the Pyrénées-Orientales, the Gironde, the Paris metropolitan region, the Alps, and the Var. That’s left nearly all of the firefighters in Guilloteau’s firehouse, which has forty-five professional fighters and around a hundred volunteers, close to the legal limits for work in a year. Professional firefighters in France, like all government employees, are capped at 1,607 hours a year, which works out to thirty-five hours a week. Across Bouches-du-Rhône there are around 1,400 professional firefighters. However, Guilloteau says that the General Confederation of Labor (CGT) union for the département has determined that they need to hire three hundred more professionals to “guarantee the safety of all citizens.” One concrete example of the dangers a lack of manpower can present comes from the ocean. The mistral — ocean winds that come howling off the seas at speeds of up to eighty miles per hour — can blow what would be manageable fires into deadly blazes, which race across the Mediterranean coast at up to four miles per hour. Firefighters in Bouches-du-Rhône have a “rule of 30.” When the outside temperature is over 30°C (80°F), when the wind speed reaches thirty kilometers per hour (18.6 miles per hour), and when humidity is around 30 percent, there’s a high chance of a fire breaking out. In conditions like these, the firefighters try to proactively combat potential fires by reinforcing the number of personnel and trucks they have ready to go across fire-sensitive areas. But when the wind comes, Guilloteau says there just aren’t enough firefighters to fight all the fires. Volunteer Your Firefighters The year 2026 is the first Bruno Ménard can remember when local-level authorities in each département denied requests to send their firefighters to other parts of France. This unprecedented geographical distribution of fires has left the départements skittish about sending much-needed personnel to other regions to fight the flames, said Ménard, who is president of the volunteer firefighters’ union. These two hundred thousand volunteers represent about three-quarters of France’s overall firefighting force. That seems like a lot, but Ménard explained that there’s a manpower shortage when it comes to the voluntary brigades too, even though they recruit between twenty and thirty thousand volunteers per year. There are a few reasons for that. But high on the list, Ménard says, is a sense of being let down that many volunteer firefighters feel after being on the job for a while. Demands like being available for a hundred hours a month, abysmally low pay of €0.80 an hour while on standby waiting to fight a fire, as well as active and ongoing training commitments, all contribute to pushing badly needed volunteer firefighters away from the calling. “It’s almost a second job,” Ménard told me. While the time commitments can be substantial and the physical dangers serious, volunteer firefighters don’t enjoy workplace protections that let them claim workers’ compensation for injuries sustained in the line of duty. They can even be fired from their day jobs if those injuries prevent them from doing their work. “It wears you out,” says Landes-based volunteer Hureaux. “We’re finding it harder and harder to keep our volunteer firefighters.” Volunteers, Hureaux adds, aren’t trying to replace professionals. The principle of signing up as a volunteer should mean that you contribute time when you have it. The trouble is that, with so much demand for firefighters right now and the consistent personnel shortages, they often feel obliged to show up so their comrades aren’t left with the burden. “Within a few years it weighs too heavy on people, and unfortunately they throw in the towel,” Hureaux said. “‘Okay, I quit.’” Despite this, the government’s latest concern to push through austerity measures means there’s no money to hire new firefighters even where there are professionals available who have completed the necessary training. At the same time, Ménard says, the government is refusing to even get around the table and look at volunteers’ demands. “If they don’t start negotiating, we’ll get out our atomic weapon,” Ménard said, pointing to a recent European Union directive that instructed member states to pay volunteer firefighters the same as professional ones. “If they don’t listen to us, we’ll demand they pay us the same amount,” Ménard promised, explaining that those figures were estimated at between €6–€8 billion additional spending per year. “We’ll blow up the public finances.”
